source.title: Public Source at 15: Showing up in our communities

text:
Halle Stockton, editor-in-chief for Pittsburgh’s Public Source, listens to community members during Public Source’s “You Have the Floor” town halls, March 18, 2026, at Local Remedy Brewing in Oakmont. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)

Saturday, Sept. 19: Showing up for our community, in person

Community engagement is inherent in local reporting, but we want it to extend beyond the conversations and interactions tied to a particular story. We want our journalists to be present in the communities we cover, not only as reporters but as neighbors, so people know who we are, and we better understand the issues and concerns shaping their lives. We hold ourselves to a high standard in this area for several reasons.

First, we know that building relationships and trust with people in our community makes for better reporting, both immediately and in the long term. Research consistently shows that nearly 80% of people have never interacted directly with a journalist. When those connections happen more frequently, residents know someone they can go to for help getting their questions answered in the future. When the journalist needs to speak with someone who knows a particular subject or place well, they have a more diverse base of sources to approach for information.

We also believe that intentional community engagement is just the right thing to do. Our community deserves respect and genuine connection. Interactions with our neighbors aren’t simply a source of story leads; they help us understand the struggles, strengths and perspectives of the place we live in a deeper way. They build trust and empathy. They reaffirm why this work is worth doing.

That’s why, in 2024, we began tracking our newsroom’s community engagement. We expect each member of our team to complete three community engagement activities per quarter, separate from interactions they have while directly pursuing a story. We’ve logged over 360 activities since then.

Some of these activities take the form of events specifically focused on listening to the community, including our seven town halls in seven days this spring, listening sessions in specific neighborhoods, and co-hosting town hall debates for candidates for elected office.

But many activities are on a smaller, more informal scale. Here are just a few types of engagement activities that our team has had.

Attending farmer’s markets, where we chatted with residents and community leaders and handed out free copies of our neighborhood zine

Participating in regular meetings of Pittsburgh’s cross-newsroom Media Advisory Committee, where residents interface with journalists to provide feedback on media coverage

Presenting about news literacy at a local professional development session for educators

Holding neighborhood walkabouts, where staff hit the streets, get familiar with local businesses and community resources, and get to know residents through casual conversation

Hosting “Coffee and Conversations” networking events that brought groups together by industry, geography or interest to have meaningful discussions on topics including real estate, the nonprofit field, southern communities, youth and disability, and more

Tabling at community events with a wide range of themes, including lectures, filmmaking, resource fairs, sports, biking and pedestrian fairs

Presenting at lifelong learning classes for older adults held in partnership with a local university

Holding community-facing workshops on storytelling, zine making and using data to answer questions about your neighborhood.

If you have a suggestion for how we can engage with your community, we’d love to hear about it. Send us an email at info@publicsource.org to let us know.

If you value this approach to journalism, help us keep doing it. We’re celebrating 15 years by raising $15,000 in 15 days. Donate now and help us reach our goal.

Volunteers at a Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank emergency drive-up food distribution in Duquesne in April 2020. (Photo by Kimberly Rowen/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)

Friday, Sept. 18: We’re with you through the everyday — and the unforgettable days

Pittsburgh’s Public Source has covered tremendous change in our region throughout the last 15 years, but few things compare to the upheaval of the COVID-19 pandemic.

When the world abruptly changed in March 2020, Public Source shifted to a fully remote newsroom and worked tirelessly to ensure our community had credible, timely information to navigate an uncertain and rapidly shifting environment — free from a paywall.

Our reporting provided updates on a daily basis, tracking the rise in local cases and documenting the community’s transition from a mandated shutdown. We also looked at the impact on Pittsburgh and its residents, students, businesses and essential workers. As the pandemic evolved, so did our coverage — from critical information on vaccines and the ongoing effects on communities, to publishing diverse firsthand perspectives.

When the stakes were high and our region needed a trusted source of information, Public Source was there. And we’ll continue to show up when our region has important questions or faces change — whether the issue is emerging health concerns, access to food and housing, government decisions that affect daily life or anything else that matters to you. But we can’t do it without you.

We’re celebrating 15 years by raising $15,000 in 15 days. Donate now and help us reach our goal.

People descend the steps of the Allegheny County Courthouse in downtown Pittsburgh, July 9, 2025. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)

Thursday, Sept. 17: 15 years of holding powerful interests accountable

Local journalism is essential to accountability, whether it’s city government, a small-town council, an academic institution or a corporation. Since 2011, Pittsburgh’s Public Source reporters have been asking hard questions and following the facts and the money to understand the systems shaping people’s everyday lives.

Here’s just some of the people and entities we’ve held to account:

2014: The nonprofit status of the NFL. What the city and county governments pay their employees (an annual installment)

2016: A public utility, which narrowly avoided catastrophic failures

2017: A local university that updated its honor code to remove zero-tolerance policies around self-harm and suicide after our reporting on it

2021: Allegheny County Jail, where restraint chairs were used on incarcerated people more than at any other county jail in the state

2021: A locally headquartered bank with a national footprint and ownership of housing communities that had unsafe conditions

2023: Operators of a local juvenile detention facility faced with extensive safety complaints

2023: The local housing authority accused of “placing vulnerable people at risk of homelessness”

2026: Police and officials in Springdale, an Allegheny County borough where debates over ICE and data centers have resulted in arrests and calls for resignation

2026: The Allegheny County Sheriff’s Office, which we challenged in court over the withholding of law enforcement names.

A coal barge heads up the Monongahela River past the downtown Pittsburgh skyline as seen from the West End Overlook Park in July 2025. Light is refracted on the left from a piece of glass. (Photo by Stephanie Strasburg/PublicSource)

Wednesday, Sept. 16: 15 years of Pittsburgh’s Public Source, by the numbers

We started in 2011 as a tiny publication that operated out of Pittsburgh Filmmakers’ Oakland office. Over the past 15 years, we’ve grown into an award-winning independent, nonprofit newsroom trusted by readers across the Pittsburgh region and recognized both locally and nationally for our impactful coverage.

And while our story is about much more than numbers, the numbers help to illustrate just how far we’ve come. For instance…

THEN: We started with just two full-time staff members in 2011.

NOW: We now have a staff of 16 full-time employees, plus several interns each semester.

THEN: 27 people donated to Public Source in 2015, the year we became a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and began accepting gifts.

NOW: We have 1,500+ current Public Source members — donors who have given at least once in the past 12 months.

Here’s some other numbers worth noting:

4,700+ stories published.

Over 360 community engagement activities by Public Source team members since we began tracking in 2024.

170+ combined years of professional experience across our full-time staff.

121 interns trained by Public Source, helping prepare the next generation of journalists.

5 neighborhood zines published since last year, with more to come.

Help us keep growing. Your gift today will help Public Source continue covering the stories that matter to our region, reaching more readers and finding new ways to engage with our community.

We’re celebrating 15 years by raising $15,000 in 15 days. Will you help us reach our goal with a gift today?

A woman and her son outside a Pittsburgh polling station on Election Day 2019. (Photo by Jay Manning/Pittsburgh’s Public Source)

Tuesday, Sept. 15: Supporting democracy in our region for 15 years

Pittsburgh’s Public Source is turning 15! To celebrate, we’re launching a campaign today to raise $15,000 for our nonprofit newsroom — in just 15 days.

We’re kicking it off on the International Day of Democracy, a day established by the United Nations to reflect on the state of democracy around the world and the role all of us play in strengthening it.

Since 2011, Public Source has supported a healthy democracy in Southwestern Pennsylvania by giving people the information they need to participate in civic life. Our journalism helps residents vote, engage in public meetings and advocate for their neighborhoods, while holding powerful people and institutions accountable.

Here are some of the ways we do this:

Preparing readers for the polls with voter guides for state and local elections

Covering the local impact of federal policies, from federal immigration crackdowns to higher education funding cuts

Shining a light on public spending by analyzing local government payroll data — and challenging institutions when they withhold information that should be available under state law

When you support Public Source, you help make this reporting possible and ensure that it remains free and available to all — because democracy works best when everyone has the information they need to participate.

Make a gift today to help us reach our $15,000 anniversary goal and keep our vital public service going for the next 15 years.

DONATE NOW

MORE STORIES

Help us continue telling stories like this one.

We’re Pittsburgh’s Public Source, an independent, nonprofit newsroom. That means we rely on donations from readers like you to help us report accurate, timely and impactful stories for the Pittsburgh region — available to everyone without paywalls.

Everyone deserves access to credible information to understand and help shape the region they call home, which is why we work hard everyday to deliver fact-checked stories on education, environment, health, local government and more.

We've seen our journalism prompt widespread change in the Pittsburgh region — but none of it would be possible without the support of our community. If you found this story valuable, consider "paying it forward" by making a gift today.
